clinicalPearls: Caused by variants in MAT1A affecting the liver-specific isoenzymes (MAT I and MAT III) that convert methionine to S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)
The commonest cause of isolated persistent hypermethioninaemia and a frequent incidental finding on newborn screening
Most individuals are clinically well; the biochemical abnormality is usually benign and does not require intervention
Reduced SAM production, with an elevated methionine but normal or low SAM, helps separate it from GNMT deficiency where SAM is high
A distinctive boiled-cabbage or sulphurous breath odour may occur from dimethyl sulfide when methionine is very high
Rare individuals with severe biallelic disease can develop neurological signs and central demyelination, attributed to SAM deficiency
Inheritance is usually autosomal recessive for the severe forms and autosomal dominant for the common mild elevation
Where treatment is considered in severe cases it is generic, such as a moderately methionine-restricted diet or SAM supplementation
reference.pathophysiology: Methionine adenosyltransferase catalyses the first step of methionine metabolism, forming S-adenosylmethionine, the principal biological methyl donor. MAT1A encodes the isoenzymes expressed mainly in the liver; when their activity is reduced, methionine is not efficiently converted and accumulates in blood, while hepatic SAM formation falls. Because MAT II activity in other tissues is preserved, most methylation reactions continue and patients are typically asymptomatic. In the uncommon severe forms, marked SAM deficiency in the nervous system is thought to impair myelin methylation reactions, giving rise to demyelination and neurological features.
additionalDifferentials: Classical homocystinuria (cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency), which also raises methionine but with homocystinuria
Hypermethioninaemia secondary to liver disease or high methionine/protein intake
additionalInvestigations: Plasma amino acids demonstrating isolated raised methionine
Plasma total homocysteine to exclude homocystinuria
S-adenosylmethionine and S-adenosylhomocysteine measurement to distinguish related disorders
Liver function tests to exclude hepatic causes
Brain MRI in the rare cases with neurological signs to assess for demyelination
redFlags: Emerging neurological signs or developmental regression suggesting a severe biallelic form with demyelination
Very high plasma methionine sustained over time
Failure of methionine to normalise, prompting search for an alternative diagnosis
Coexisting hepatic dysfunction pointing to a different or additional cause
reference.prognosis: The great majority have an entirely benign course with normal development and lifespan; only the rare severe biallelic forms carry a risk of neurological impairment, which may improve with dietary or SAM treatment.
pitfalls: Mislabelling isolated hypermethioninaemia as classical homocystinuria and imposing unnecessary treatment
Failing to check homocysteine and SAM/SAH, which are needed to place the disorder correctly
Over-restricting methionine in a well child, risking deficiency of an essential amino acid
Assuming all cases are benign without excluding the rare severe form when neurological signs appear
references: Mudd SH. Hypermethioninemias of genetic and non-genetic origin
Blau N. Physician's Guide to the Diagnosis, Treatment, and Follow-up of Inherited Metabolic Diseases
management: Reassure and avoid intervention in the great majority, in whom isolated persistent hypermethioninaemia is a benign incidental finding
Confirm the diagnosis by excluding homocystinuria and other causes of hypermethioninaemia through homocysteine and metabolite measurement
For the rare severe biallelic disease with neurological involvement, institute a methionine-restricted diet and consider oral S-adenosylmethionine supplementation
Monitor plasma methionine and undertake neurological review and brain MRI where central demyelination is suspected
Involve a metabolic dietitian in symptomatic or severe cases
Offer genetic counselling for MAT1A variants, recognising both dominant and recessive inheritance patterns
